c.tagline: Shikoku's easygoing capital — Japan's oldest hot spring, a hilltop castle, and the haiku of Masaoka Shiki.

taxi.fareNote: Ride-hailing here (GO, Uber, DiDi) only dispatches licensed, metered taxis rather than private cars, and street/rank taxis are plentiful and all run on the meter.

emergency.note: 110 reaches police; 119 reaches fire and ambulance. English support is limited on local lines, but the 24/7 Japan Visitor Hotline (050-3816-2787) offers translation help.

hood_desc: Matsuyama's ancient hot-spring quarter, built around the 1894 Dogo Onsen Honkan bathhouse said to have inspired Spirited Away; ryokan, foot baths, the Botchan clock and a covered shopping street make it the city's most atmospheric place to stay.

The downtown twin arcades of Okaido and Gintengai form Matsuyama's main shopping and nightlife zone, thick with restaurants, izakaya, department stores and bars, all beneath the castle hill and on the tram loop.

The gentle strip at the foot of Matsuyama Castle along Ropeway Street, lined with cafes and craft shops and leading to the ropeway and chairlift up to the hilltop keep; central and ideal for sightseeing.

The district around Matsuyama City Station, the Iyotetsu hub with the Takashimaya department store and its rooftop Ferris wheel; a lively, convenient shopping area and terminus for suburban trains and buses.
The quieter neighbourhood around JR Matsuyama Station, handy for travellers connecting by JR limited express, with business hotels and everyday eateries a couple of tram stops from the centre.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, as throughout Japan.

transit.hours: Trams and buses run roughly 6am to 10:30pm; taxis fill the late-night gap.
transit.pay: Tap the local ICi-Card or a nationwide Suica/ICOCA, or pay cash; the city tram is a flat ¥200 (~$1.30). The retro Botchan Ressha steam-style tram is a separate ~¥800 fare.

ferry: Matsuyama Kanko Port at Takahama (Hiroshima ferry/hydrofoil; night ferries to Kobe & Kitakyushu)

transit.m: Iyotetsu limousine bus to Matsuyama City Station, JR Station & Dogo Onsen, ~15-40 min
Local Iyotetsu bus route 52 into the city centre

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in Japan and can cause confusion; attentive service is standard and already included.

food.name: Taimeshi (sea bream rice)
food.desc: Ehime's pride, either whole sea bream cooked in a kamameshi pot of rice or, Uwajima style, raw slices dipped in egg-and-soy and poured over rice.

places.name: Uotake
places.note: Local favourite for tai kamameshi using sea bream from the Uwa Sea.

places.name: Kadoya Okaido Branch
places.note: Long-established Matsuyama restaurant serving taimeshi alongside its famous udon.

places.name: Goshiki
places.note: Relaxed set-menu restaurant whose Matsuyama taimeshi set is a reliable introduction.

food.name: Jakoten
food.desc: Small whole fish from the Uwa Sea ground bones and all into a paste and deep-fried into a savoury brown fishcake, eaten hot with grated ginger.

places.name: Uotake
places.note: Serves jakoten fresh-fried as part of its wide Ehime specialty menu.

places.name: Dogo Haikara-dori arcade
places.note: Covered shopping street between the station and the bathhouse, several jakoten stalls.

places.name: Okaido and Gintengai arcades
places.note: Central shopping arcades with standing counters frying jakoten to order.

food.name: Nabeyaki udon
food.desc: Matsuyama's own soft udon served in a small aluminium pot in sweet, pale broth with beef, egg and fishcake - a local lunch since the postwar years.

places.name: Kadoya Okaido Branch
places.note: One of the two historic Matsuyama nabeyaki udon houses, open since the 1940s.

places.name: Asahi
places.note: The other classic nabeyaki udon shop, famously simple and quick.

places.name: Goshiki
places.note: Serves udon and noodle sets hot or cold alongside its rice bowls.

food.name: Satsuma-jiru
food.desc: Grilled white fish pounded with miso, thinned with dashi and poured cold over hot barley rice with spring onion and cucumber; a fisherman's summer dish.

places.name: Uotake
places.note: Traditional Ehime home cooking including the cold miso-and-fish rice bowl.

places.name: Goshiki
places.note: Local-cuisine set menus that rotate through Ehime country dishes.

places.name: Nikitatsu-an
places.note: Restaurant inside a working sake brewery pairing regional dishes with its own sake.

food.name: Goshiki somen
food.desc: Five-coloured wheat noodles - plain, green tea, egg, buckwheat and pink shiso - a Matsuyama specialty made since the Edo period and served chilled.

places.name: Goshiki
places.note: The restaurant of the family that has made five-coloured somen in Matsuyama for generations.

places.name: Okaido and Gintengai arcades
places.note: Souvenir shops sell boxed goshiki somen to take home.

places.name: Dogo Haikara-dori arcade
places.note: Noodle and confectionery shops lining the route to the old bathhouse.

food.name: Botchan dango
food.desc: Three balls of sweet bean paste - green tea, egg yolk and red azuki - stacked on a skewer, named for Soseki's novel set in Matsuyama.

places.name: Tsuboya Kashiho
places.note: Historic confectioner near the bathhouse credited with creating Botchan dango.

places.name: Ichiroku Honpo
places.note: Famous Ehime sweet maker for both Botchan dango and rolled taruto cake.

places.name: Dogo Haikara-dori arcade
places.note: Tea houses along the arcade serve dango with green tea after the baths.

food.name: Ehime mikan juice
food.desc: Pure pressed mandarin juice from Japan's top citrus prefecture, so central here that some taps genuinely pour orange juice instead of water.

places.name: 10 FACTORY
places.note: Mikan juice bar with single-variety citrus juices and sorbet by the cup.

places.name: Dogo Onsen Station area
places.note: Kiosks and the celebrated mikan juice tap near the station entrance.

places.name: Okaido arcade
places.note: Citrus stands and souvenir shops selling bottled Ehime mikan juice.

food.name: Ehime sake
food.desc: Soft-water sake brewed with Shikoku rice, often light and dry to match the local seafood; several breweries sit within Matsuyama itself.

places.name: Nikitatsu-an
places.note: Restaurant and shop of Mizuguchi Shuzo, tasting the brewery's sake beside Dogo Onsen.

places.name: Ninomaru and Okaido izakaya
places.note: Central bar district where izakaya stock Ehime labels by the glass.

places.name: Dogo Haikara-dori arcade
places.note: Sake shops offering tasting flights of Ehime breweries.

landmarks: Dogo Onsen Honkan
Japan's most storied bathhouse, a creaking 1894 wooden castle of steam said to have inspired Studio Ghibli's 'Spirited Away'.
Matsuyama Castle
One of Japan's twelve original-keep castles rides a 132-meter hilltop, reached by ropeway and rewarding visitors with Seto Inland Sea views.
Ishite-ji Temple
Temple 51 of the Shikoku pilgrimage, a National Treasure-filled complex of Kamakura-era gates, pagodas and mysterious candlelit caves.
Isaniwa Shrine
A vermilion 17th-century shrine above Dogo, one of only three built in the ornate Hachiman style, reached by a grand stone stairway.
Botchan Karakuri Clock
Dogo's whimsical mechanical clock springs to life on the hour, parading characters from Natsume Soseki's beloved novel 'Botchan'.
Bansuiso Villa
A surprising 1922 French-Renaissance château built by a count-turned-diplomat, now an elegant cultural venue beneath Matsuyama Castle's slopes.
Ninomaru Historical Garden
Terraced water gardens tracing the footprint of the castle's former secondary compound, a tranquil spot famous with couples for its citrus courtyards.
Shiki Memorial Museum
A thoughtful museum honoring Masaoka Shiki, Matsuyama's native son who revolutionized haiku, in this self-proclaimed capital of the form.
Dogo Park (Yuzuki Castle Ruins)
The moated grounds of a medieval Kono-clan castle beside the onsen district, with reconstructed samurai residences and cherry-blossom lookouts.
Dogo Shopping Arcade (Haikara-dori)
A lantern-lit covered arcade curving from the tram terminus to the Honkan, perfect for yukata-clad strolls past craft and confectionery shops.

train.note: Japan has no international trains, and no Shinkansen reaches Shikoku. JR Shikoku's limited express Shiokaze runs from Matsuyama across the Seto-Ohashi Bridge to Okayama in about 2 hours 40 minutes, where you connect to the San'yo Shinkansen for Hiroshima, Osaka and Tokyo. The Uwakai express runs south toward Uwajima, and the private Iyotetsu tram network covers the city and Dogo Onsen. Through tickets combining the express and the Shinkansen are sold at the station and are cheaper than buying the legs separately.

bus.note: No international buses serve Japan. Highway coaches from Matsuyama City Station and JR Matsuyama Station run to Osaka, Kobe, Hiroshima via the Shimanami Kaido, Takamatsu and Kochi; JR Shikoku Bus and Iyotetsu are the main operators, with overnight runs to Tokyo. The Hiroshima coach takes about 4 hours 30 minutes versus 70 minutes by hydrofoil, so the boat usually wins. Willer Express (https://willerexpress.com/en/) sells some Shikoku routes online in English.

intl.to: Hiroshima (Japan) - sails from Matsuyama Kanko Port at Takahama, about 20 min by Iyotetsu train from the centre
Kobe, Osaka & Kitakyushu (Japan) - overnight sailings from Matsuyama Kanko Port
intl.op: Setonaikai Kisen and partner lines (tickets at the Matsuyama Kanko Port terminal; no verified booking URL)

ferry.note: Matsuyama has no scheduled international ferries. From Matsuyama Kanko Port at Takahama, the Superjet hydrofoil reaches Hiroshima in about 70 minutes and the slower cruise ferry in around 2 hours 40 minutes, operated by Setonaikai Kisen with Ishizaki Kisen. Overnight ferries also run to Kobe, Osaka and Kitakyushu, arriving next morning with cabins available. Cruise-ferry frequencies have been reduced in recent years, so check the current timetable rather than assuming an evening sailing.

full.name: Kotohira (Konpira-san)

full.blurb: Shikoku's other big city, home to the exquisite Ritsurin Garden and the jumping-off point for the Seto Inland Sea art islands.
full.name: Takamatsu

full.blurb: Cross the Seto Inland Sea by ferry or hydrofoil to the Peace Memorial Park and, nearby, the floating torii of Miyajima.
full.name: Hiroshima

half.blurb: A preserved merchant town about 40 minutes by train, with wax-trade mansions, a restored kabuki theatre and streets of Edo-era townhouses.
half.name: Uchiko

half.blurb: The gateway to the island-hopping Shimanami Kaido cycle route across the Seto Inland Sea, plus Imabari Castle and world-famous towels.
half.name: Imabari & Shimanami Kaido

half.blurb: A riverside 'little Kyoto' castle town about an hour away, known for its rebuilt wooden keep and summer cormorant fishing.
half.name: Ozu
